t: Introduction: topic and learning objectives
n: In this lecture we shall consider the bioethics of cloning and stem cells. The development of biomedicine and biotechnology has given rise to complex questions: the cloning of human cells, genetic testing and stem cells. Stem cells are obtained mainly from the human embryo, so the dispute over the status of the embryo has become one of the most acute bioethical issues. Outline of the class: the concept of cloning, the Dolly experiment, therapeutic and reproductive cloning, sources of stem cells, and the approach of religions and states.

t: The concept and term "cloning"
n: Cloning, in English cloning, is the reproduction of an object in exactly the same form. The objects obtained as a result are called clones. The term derives from a Greek word and means a branch, a twig, an offshoot. In biology the term is used in two senses: natural origination, or obtaining genetically identical organisms by asexual reproduction. Attention: a clone, that is, the resulting copy organism, and cloning, that is, the process of obtaining it, are not the same thing. Do not confuse them.

t: Difference between sexual reproduction and cloning
n: Let us consider the difference between sexual reproduction and cloning. In a gamete the chromosomes are in a haploid set, so it cannot by itself develop into a new organism. In fertilisation two gametes fuse, and a zygote and a new genome are formed. Therefore the mother is not fully reproduced in the offspring. Only if the mother's genetic information is passed on unchanged can organisms that fully reproduce her be obtained. Cloning envisages precisely this situation.

t: Natural clones: monozygotic twins
n: Clones also occur in nature. If a zygote divides at an early stage, the genome of the two children is identical. Monozygotic twins are true clones: they are of the same sex and very similar, their genome is identical, that is, they are a natural clone. In dizygotic twins, by contrast, the genotype differs, the sex may differ from that of monozygotic twins, they are not identical, and the text does not call them clones.

t: Blastomeres and totipotency in plants
n: The embryo of mammals, including humans, at an early stage of development, up to the 8-blastomere stage, can be harmlessly divided into separate blastomeres. Under certain conditions, individuals with the same genotype may arise from these blastomeres, like monozygotic twins. For example, from a single 8-cell embryo, 8 absolutely identical boys or 8 girls could be born. In plants cloning is widespread; this is vegetative reproduction. Their cells do not lose totipotency, that is, the ability to realise all the information contained in the nucleus.

t: Case analysis: twins and the clone
n: Case analysis. Situation: a single zygote divided at an early stage, and as a result two brothers were born. Their genome is identical. Question: why are they considered a natural clone, and what distinguishes them from artificial cloning? Answer: because their genome is identical. Natural birth is morally irreproachable; the objection is directed only at the technique of artificial nuclear transfer. Attention: a clone does not mean an identical person. Only the genotype is reproduced; character and abilities are formed in upbringing, and appearance too may differ.

t: Quick question: basics of cloning
n: Let us review the basics of cloning. What is a clone? Reproducing an object in exactly the same form is called cloning, and the resulting object is called a clone. Why is cloning widespread in plants? Because their cells do not lose totipotency, that is, the ability to bring into play all the information in the nucleus. Why are monozygotic twins a natural clone? When the zygote divides early, their genome is identical, and both are of the same sex. Attention: monozygotic, that is, identical twins, not dizygotic twins. Only the former are true clones; the genome of the latter is not identical.

t: History of cloning: from Lopashov to Gurdon
n: The history of cloning begins with the method of nuclear transfer in frogs proposed by the Russian embryologist Lopashov in the 1940s. In 1962 Gurdon took as the nuclear donor not a germ cell but a specialised epithelial cell from the intestine of a tadpole. In the late 1970s the difficulty in mammals was overcome. In 1996 the sheep Dolly was created, that is, a clone of an adult animal. All of today's cloning experiments are based on this method of nuclear transfer.

t: Stages of the nuclear transfer method
n: The nuclear transfer method consists of several stages. First, the nucleus of a somatic cell is taken and isolated. The egg cell is enucleated, that is, its nucleus is removed. Then the nucleus is placed into the egg, and a reconstructed egg is obtained, from which the clone organism develops. The mammalian egg is a thousand times smaller than that of amphibians, which is why the transition was difficult. In Dolly's case the nuclear donor was a mammary gland cell culture, of the Finn Dorset breed.

t: Difficulties of cloning in mammals
n: The egg cell of mammals is a thousand times smaller than that of amphibians. For this reason the transition from amphibians to mammals was difficult. These difficulties were overcome by the end of the 1970s. In the early 1980s mouse embryos were cloned, and at the end of the 1980s domestic rabbits and large domestic animals were cloned. Attention: an amphibian and a mammal are not the same; they differ in the size of the egg cell.

t: Dolly the sheep: the first mammalian clones
n: In 1996 the story of the cloning of the sheep Dolly at the firm PPL Therapeutics in Scotland caused a sensation. A group of scientists led by Ian Wilmut created a cloned animal, that is, Dolly, from the somatic cells of an adult animal. In the textbook Dolly is given as the first mammalian clones. The nuclear donor was taken from the Finn Dorset breed. Until the mid-1990s the question of using large mammals as nuclear donors had practically not been posed. Some scientists believed that human cloning was only 10 years away.

t: How Dolly was created
n: How was Dolly created? Dolly arose from a reconstructed egg cell. The nuclear donor was a mammary gland cell culture from a sheep of the "Finn Dorset" breed. The method is as follows: a nucleus is isolated from the mammary gland cell culture and transferred into an anucleate, that is, enucleated, egg cell. From the resulting reconstructed egg cell the clone, that is, the sheep Dolly, develops.

t: Practical possibilities of animal cloning
n: Cloning has made it possible not only to preserve the genotype of valuable animals but also to multiply them without limit. Cloning high-yielding cows may revolutionise agriculture, since not individual copies but whole herds are created. The method also applies to breeding famous sport horses and expensive fur-bearing animals, and to preserving rare and endangered animals. Attention: interspecies nuclear transfer may open new prospects for rescuing species on the verge of extinction, but this is not yet a guaranteed result.

t: Case analysis: Dolly and public questions
n: Case analysis. Situation: in 1996, at the firm PPL Therapeutics, Scotland, Ian Wilmut's group created a cloned sheep nicknamed Dolly from the somatic cells of an adult sheep. Dolly arose from a reconstructed egg cell, the nuclear donor being a mammary gland cell culture from a sheep of the "Finn Dorset" breed. According to the supposition of some scientists, human cloning was only 10 years away. This posed a number of ethical and philosophical questions to the public. Question: why did society become alarmed after Dolly was created? What does it mean that a clone was obtained from the somatic cell of an adult animal?

t: Human cloning: no proven fact
n: To this day there is no proven fact of human cloning. The main aim of human cloning is to obtain personal embryonic stem cells and organs and tissues grown from them; this is called therapeutic cloning. Reproductive cloning, that is, growing a mature organism, is a secondary task. It is considered from the standpoint of solving the problem of infertility. Attention: therapeutic and reproductive cloning are not the same. It is reproductive cloning that has given rise to many moral problems and prejudices.

t: Therapeutic and reproductive cloning
n: At present the main aim of cloning is not the reproductive but the therapeutic direction, that is, obtaining embryonic stem cells. In therapeutic cloning, personal stem cells, organs and tissues are obtained. Its ethical problem is the status of the embryo and pressure on women, and legal decisions differ between countries. In therapeutic cloning a 14-day embryo is used, so questions arise about the status of the embryo. Reproductive cloning is the growing of a mature organism. It has given rise to numerous moral problems and prejudices, and is prohibited in many countries.

t: Biomedical reasons for prohibiting cloning
n: There are biomedical reasons for prohibiting cloning. The methods of animal cloning are imperfect: mortality among embryos and newborns is high, so transferring the experiment to humans is unacceptable. When cells are grown in a test tube, various mutations appear, and the number of people with genetic defects may increase. The result of cloning is not the child of the parents but their twin, which gives rise to new moral and legal problems. Supporters see it as a method for those who cannot pass on their own gene, while the prohibition is assessed as halting a whole scientific direction.

t: Attention: the genotype is cloned, not the personality
n: Attention: the genotype is cloned, not the personality. Critics of reproductive cloning forget that only the genotype, that is, the organism itself, is cloned. A person's personality is formed in the process of upbringing and acquiring knowledge. Such conditions cannot be reproduced exactly. Monozygotic, that is, identical twins brought up in different conditions are natural clones. Their character, inclinations and intellectual abilities differ. Even with an identical genotype, outward appearance often does not match.

t: The naturalness of cloning and the essence of the objections
n: One can speak of the naturalness of cloning only because the birth of monozygotic twins is natural. Such cloning of the human genome, occurring naturally, is ethically irreproachable. There is nothing improper in the birth of twins. The objection arises with artificial transfer of the nucleus. Consequently, the objection depends not on the fact of cloning itself but on the technical features of the method. In cases where ordinary medicine is powerless, cloning technologies may help people to have children.

t: Genetic determinism and the "dictatorship of normality"
n: Exaggerating the role of genes removes personal responsibility. There is a danger of regarding giftedness, defects and deviations as determined by heredity. Genetic determinism may contradict the idea of free will and responsibility; courts usually do not accept such arguments. Everyone has many genes that deviate from the average "norm", so the risk of a "dictatorship of normality" is real. It is linked with discrimination and racist stereotype. Reductionism, in turn, may lead to viewing the human being as a collection of molecules organised in a particular way.

t: Prohibitions on human cloning and the UNESCO declaration
n: Reproductive cloning is the growing of a mature organism, and many moral problems arose precisely from it. The UNESCO declaration prohibits cloning for the purpose of reproducing the human species, since it is contrary to human dignity. The European protocol prohibits human cloning and entered into force in 2002. In many countries national laws impose a complete or temporary ban. The prohibition relates to reproductive cloning; the question of therapeutic cloning has not yet been resolved. The other questions are at the discretion of each state, and international guidance is unclear.

t: Quick question: human cloning
n: Let us review the questions on human cloning. What is the main aim of therapeutic cloning? To obtain personal embryonic stem cells and organs and tissues grown from them. What is reproductive cloning? The growing of a mature organism; it is considered from the standpoint of solving the problem of infertility. What does the UNESCO declaration prohibit? Cloning for the purpose of reproducing the human species. Attention: therapeutic and reproductive cloning are not the same; their aims and prohibitive status differ.

t: Case analysis: the dilemma of therapeutic cloning
n: Case analysis. Situation: scientists request permission for therapeutic cloning in order to treat serious, so far incurable diseases such as Parkinson's or Alzheimer's disease. Cloning by nuclear transfer leads to the creation of a peculiar "embryo" intended only for obtaining stem cells. Question: if permission is given and the technology is created, would this not lead to cloning for the purpose of producing offspring? The counter-argument is that in cloning only the genotype is reproduced, while the personality is formed in the process of upbringing and acquiring knowledge.

t: Four ways of artificially obtaining an embryo
n: At present there are four main ways of artificially obtaining embryos. The first is the transfer into the uterus of an embryo obtained by IVF, that is, in vitro fertilisation; the second is the "surplus" embryos obtained for implantation. Two further ways are an embryo obtained by fertilisation for research or for obtaining stem cells, and an embryo created by transferring a nucleus into an egg cell. In the first way, attempts that prevent the realisation of the embryo's potential are rejected, except for risk to the mother's life. Embryos created for research or use require special consideration.

t: Sources of stem cells
n: The main aim of therapeutic cloning is to obtain personal embryonic stem cells and organs and tissues grown from them. There are several sources: the mature organism, umbilical cord blood, foetal tissue and embryonic tissue. It is acknowledged by all that the largest source of stem cells for therapeutic purposes is embryos. A stem cell can turn into anything, so the consequences are difficult to foresee.

t: Totipotent and pluripotent cells
n: Individual cells of an early preimplantation embryo can be removed without harm. This is one of the solutions to the problem of obtaining stem cells. If the cells are totipotent, that is, able to turn into any organ or an independent body, they are in essence separate zygotes and embryos and are protected like the original embryos. If the cells are only pluripotent, they are not regarded as an embryo. Their use does not offend those who regard the embryo as a human being. Whether a cell is totipotent or pluripotent can be determined only retrospectively, that is, by observing it afterwards.

t: Embryo status, 14 days and women's rights
n: In therapeutic cloning a 14-day embryo is used. The question arose of up to what time an embryo may be regarded as an embryo and not as a human being. In Great Britain it has been specially established that the age of the embryo is at most 14 days from the moment of fusion of the germ cells. If embryonic material and umbilical cord blood become a source, women may come under particular pressure. The European ethics group regards this as a matter of first-order importance. Attention: the International Bioethics Committee at UNESCO has not reached a single opinion on creating and using an embryo. Decisions differ between states.

t: Views of religions: Islam and Judaism
n: Religions regard the embryo differently. Islam holds that the embryo has no soul as yet and permits the use of the human embryo up to 40 days after fertilisation. In Judaism the fertilised egg cell is not yet a human being; it becomes one in the course of development inside the mother. An embryo developing outside the mother's body is equated with a gamete, and once implanted in the mother it is regarded as a being. In a pluralistic world such differences are inevitable: what is permitted in Buddhism may be impermissible in Christianity, and vice versa.

t: Views of religions: branches of Christianity
n: What is permitted in Buddhism may be impermissible in Christianity, and vice versa. Christian churches regard the embryo differently. The Roman Catholic Church takes the strictest position: it holds that a human being appears from the moment of fertilisation. According to the Protestant view, the embryo is not a full human being. In the Russian Orthodox Church the foetus is regarded as a human being and a person from the moment of conception. Attention: the Protestant view differs from the Catholic one and is itself not uniform.

t: Great Britain: legal regulation
n: Great Britain has been a leader in legal regulation. It was the first in Europe to approve stem cell research subject to special precautions. This chain begins with the Embryology Act of 1990. The opinion of an expert group was expressed in August 2000, and then the chambers of parliament approved it. The HFEA, that is, the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority, regulates the research. At first the permission was limited to the study of infertility. Now the list of purposes has been extended and includes stem cell research.

t: Embryo research in European countries
n: In many states of the European Union there is no law on embryonic stem cells at all. The laws range from an absolute ban to permission to create embryos for research. In France, Germany and Ireland, research on the embryo is prohibited. In Spain, Finland and Sweden, research is possible on surplus embryos. In Belgium and the Netherlands there is no legal framework, yet research takes place. In Portugal there is neither law nor research. In many countries a similarity is seen between embryo research and abortion.

t: Similarity between embryo research and abortion
n: In many countries a similarity is being found between embryo research and the question of abortion. In both cases the issue is the status of the embryo. The Constitution of Ireland affirms the right to life of the unborn and equates it with the right of the mother. In the European Union this is the only such state. Abortion is possible only if the mother's life is under direct threat, but not because of rape or an embryo anomaly. This rule contradicts a decision of the European Court of Justice. Attention: whether the right in Ireland begins from fertilisation or from implantation is not clear in the source. Do not state it as an exact point in time.

t: The USA and international documents
n: In a number of US states there are laws regulating and restricting embryo research. At the federal level, the funding of research that harms the embryo is prohibited. In the Council of Europe, protection is obligatory and the creation of an embryo is prohibited. The Additional Protocol entered into force in 2002. International guidelines do not clarify the question: apart from the ban on reproductive cloning, everything else is at the discretion of each state.

t: Case analysis: the laws of different states
n: Case analysis. Situation: embryo research in Great Britain is permitted with special precautions and under the control of the HFEA, that is, the embryology authority. In Austria, Germany and France such research is prohibited. In Belgium and the Netherlands, however, it is conducted without a legal framework. Reason: religions regard the embryo differently. Islam permits it up to 40 days after fertilisation, while the Catholic Church holds that a human being begins at fertilisation. Question: why is international agreement difficult? Take into account that, apart from the ban on reproductive cloning, all questions are left to the discretion of states.

t: UNESCO Committee: three approaches
n: In the opinion of the UNESCO Bioethics Committee, the morality of research depends largely on the status of the embryo. The document indicates three kinds of moral view on embryonic stem cells. The first is an absolute ban: the use of the embryo is completely contrary to morality. The second is conditional permission: only for medical purposes and under strict conditions. The third is the view that research should be prohibited because of the risk. Attention: conditional permission is not absolute permission; under the second approach strict conditions are required.

t: Medical genetics ethics and genetic testing
n: In medical genetics, because of the patient's age or condition, the decision is taken by the parents or guardian. When a hereditary pathology is identified and the patient cannot decide himself, the decision passes to the parents or guardian. A genome defect is detected even at the asymptomatic stage of a disease, for example Alzheimer's disease or Huntington's chorea. Two questions remain: who has the right to know hereditary characteristics, and whether a pathological genotype may be changed.

t: The risk-benefit problem and stem cell treatment
n: As medical technologies have expanded, both the benefit to the patient and the degree of risk have increased. Physicians find it hard to resolve "risk-benefit" alone. Stem cells are obtained mainly from the embryo; they may be useful in restoring liver and brain function and articular cartilage. They can turn into anything, and theoretically a cancerous tumour might develop years later, but this is only a supposition. The long-term consequences have not been sufficiently studied. The Hippocratic principle "Do no harm" has become more complicated, and clinical trials do not guarantee safety.

t: Prenatal diagnosis and its ethical limit
n: Bioethics has dealt with the question of preventing the use of antenatal diagnosis, that is, diagnosis carried out during pregnancy, for non-medical purposes. An example of a non-medical purpose: determining the sex of the foetus, that is, using diagnosis so that a girl is not born. The development of science has brought new risks connected with hereditary diagnosis before implantation, that is, before the embryo becomes established in the uterus. Remember: detecting a genome defect is a medical purpose, whereas choosing the sex of the foetus is a non-medical purpose. Do not confuse the two.

t: "Made-to-order" children and parental responsibility
n: The production of embryos and children "to order" may be aimed at obtaining desired genetic characteristics. The process of human reproduction is becoming technologised. In foreign practice there have been cases where legal measures were taken against parents who refused an abortion when the child had a serious hereditary disease and disability. The American biologist B. Glass wrote in 1971 that modern biology is able to guarantee the quality of all newborns. Question: should parents be held responsible for the result of the choice? The book leaves this question open.

t: Conclusion and main findings
n: Let us sum up. In cloning only the genotype is reproduced, while the personality is formed in upbringing and acquiring knowledge. Natural clones, that is, monozygotic twins, also differ from one another. In many countries reproductive cloning is prohibited. The main aim of therapeutic cloning is to obtain embryonic stem cells, and the questions relating to it are unresolved. Stem cells offer hope for the treatment of Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis. However, clinical trials alone are not sufficient to guarantee safety. Genetic engineering has complicated the principle of "Do no harm": both benefit and risk have increased. The question of the right to know genetic information also remains open.
